docs.title: Contributing to STEMAIDE
docs.text: We love contributions! Whether you are an educator, student, or engineer, you can help us build the best open-source STEM curriculum in Africa.

docs.title: Ways to Contribute
docs.text:
1. Report Bugs: Found a typo or a broken circuit diagram? Open an issue on GitHub.
  2. Add Translations: Help us translate these guides into local languages (Twi, Ga, Ewe, Swahili, etc.).
  3. Create Missions: Design a new project and add it to the curriculum (See the Contributing to the Curriculum guide).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Fork this repository.
  2. Clone your fork.
  3. Create a branch: git checkout -b my-new-mission.
  4. Commit your changes.
  5. Push to the branch.
  6. Submit a Pull Request.

docs.title: Community Code of Conduct
docs.text: Be respectful, inclusive, and helpful. We are here to learn together.

docs.title: 6. Push Your Changes
docs.text:
Now that you’ve made and saved your changes, you’ll need to push them to your forked repository.

  1. Stage your changes:
git add .
  1. Commit your changes with a meaningful message:
git commit -m "Added contribution guide and updated changelog"
  1. Push your changes to your fork:
git push origin update-readme

docs.title: 7. Create a Pull Request
docs.text:
A pull request (PR) is how you ask to merge your changes into the main repository.

  1. Go to your forked repository on GitHub.
  2. Click on the Pull Requests tab.
  3. Click on the New Pull Request button.
  4. Select your branch (e.g., update-readme) and compare it with the main repository’s branch (usually main or master).
  5. Add a title and description for your PR:
    • Title: Added Contribution Guidelines
    • Description: Describe the changes you made, e.g., “Added detailed steps for contributing and updated the changelog.”
  6. Click Create Pull Request.

docs.title: 8. Wait for Review
docs.text:
The project maintainers will review your pull request. Here’s what might happen:

  1. Approved: Your changes will be merged into the main project!

  2. Requested Changes: Maintainers might ask for modifications. Follow their feedback and update your PR.

  3. To update your PR after feedback:

    • Make the required changes in your local branch.
    • Commit and push the changes:
    git add .
git commit -m "Fixed feedback issues"
git push origin update-readme

docs.title: Additional Tips
docs.text:
- Ask for Help: If you’re stuck, feel free to ask for help by commenting on your pull request or opening an issue.
- Test Your Changes: Ensure that your changes look correct by previewing them in your text editor or GitHub.

Congratulations! 🎉 You’ve successfully contributed to the project. Thank you for making this documentation better for everyone!

docs.title: About STEMAIDE
docs.text: Reinventing the Future. We are an EdTech startup empowering young Africans through immersive, hands-on STEM education experiences.

docs.title: Our Mission
docs.text:
We exist to equip young Africans with the 21st-century creative mindset and the technical skills they need to become the next generation of Innovators and Entrepreneurs.

We believe in a practical, hands-on approach. We don't just teach theory; we build the future.

docs.title: What Does "STEMAIDE" Stand For?
docs.text:
It is more than just an acronym. It is our pedagogical framework:

🔬 STEM

Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics. The fundamental laws of the universe and the tools to manipulate them.

🎨 Arts

Creativity is at the heart of engineering. We blend aesthetics with function to build beautiful solutions.

💡 Innovation

We don't just repeat what exists. We invent new ways to solve old problems.

📐 Design

Design Thinking is our process. Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

🚀 Entrepreneurship

We solve problems for people. We teach students to turn their inventions into viable solutions for their communities.

docs.title: 1. The Concept: Digital Output
docs.text:
What are we learning? We are going to turn on a Light Emitting Diode (LED). To do this, we need to send an electrical signal from the Arduino to the LED.

  • HIGH signal = 5V (On)
  • LOW signal = 0V (Off)

We will use a command called digitalWrite() to send this signal.

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text: LED (Any Color) Arduino Uno Breadboard Jumper Wires

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text:
Caution: LEDs have polarity! They have a positive (+) leg and a negative (-) leg.

  • Long Leg (+): Connects to the Signal (Pin 6).
  • Short Leg (-): Connects to Ground (GND).

Step 1: Insert the LED into the breadboard.

Step 2: Connect the Positive (Long Leg) to Arduino Pin 6. (Using a Red wire helps you remember it's positive!)

Step 3: Connect the Negative (Short Leg) to Arduino GND. (Using a Black or Blue wire helps you remember it's Ground!)

Step 4: Plug the Arduino into your computer using the Blue USB cable.

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Give the pin a name so it's easier to remember
int ledPin = 6;

void setup() {
  // 2. Tell Arduino that this pin is for OUTPUT (sending power out)
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 3. Turn the LED ON (HIGH voltage)
  digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
}

docs.title: Explaining the lines
docs.text:
• int ledPin = 6; -> We create a variable named ledPin and set it to 6. Now, whenever we say ledPin, the computer knows we mean Pin 6.
  • pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT); -> Pins can be inputs (listening) or outputs (talking). We want to talk to the LED, so we set it to OUTPUT.
  • digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH); -> Send 5V to the pin. Let there be light!

docs.title: 5. Upload & Test
docs.text:
1. Click Verify (Checkmark).
  2. Click Upload (Arrow).
  3. Look at your board. Is the LED on?

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• LED not turning on?
  • Try flipping the LED. Remember, the Long leg must go to Pin 6.
  • Check if the wires are pushed all the way in.
  • Check if you uploaded the code successfully (Look for "Done uploading").
  • Dim light?
  • Ensure you are using a digital pin (0-13), not an analog pin.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Congratulations! You have just built your first electronic circuit. You learned how to complete a circuit and control it with software. Next, let's make it blink!

docs.title: CONCLUSION
docs.text: In a nutshell, the project centered around five blinking LEDs offers hands-on experience in synchronized LED control. By creating a blinking pattern across all five LEDs, participants gain insights into circuit connections, loop-based programming, and coordinated timing. This endeavor serves as a stepping stone for more advanced electronics projects, highlighting the concept of repetitive actions and sparking interest in practical electronics applications.

docs.title: 1. The Concept: Making Noise
docs.text:
What are we learning? We are going to use a Buzzer to make a sound. Just like the LED, the Buzzer is a connection output.

  • HIGH signal = Sound ON (Beep!)
  • LOW signal = Sound OFF (Silence)

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text: Buzzer Arduino Uno Breadboard Jumper Wires

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text:
Caution: The Buzzer has polarity!

  • Long Leg (+): Connects to the Signal (Pin 3).
  • Short Leg (-): Connects to Ground (GND).

Step 1: Insert the Buzzer into the breadboard.

Step 2: Connect the Positive (Long Leg) to Arduino Pin 3.

Step 3: Connect the Negative (Short Leg) to Arduino GND.

Step 4: Plug in the Arduino.

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define the pin for the buzzer
int buzzerPin = 3;

void setup() {
  // 2. Set the buzzer pin as an OUTPUT
  pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 3. Turn the buzzer ON
  digitalWrite(buzzerPin, HIGH);

  // Wait for 1 second (1000 milliseconds)
  delay(1000); 

  // 4. Turn the buzzer OFF
  digitalWrite(buzzerPin, LOW);

  // Wait for 1 second 
  delay(1000);
}

docs.title: Explaining the lines
docs.text: • delay(1000); -> This pauses the program for 1000 milliseconds (which is 1 second). This creates a "Beep... Silence... Beep" pattern.

docs.title: 5. Upload & Test
docs.text:
1. Click Verify.
  2. Click Upload.
  3. Listen! Do you hear a beeping sound?

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No Sound?
  • Check the polarity (Long leg to Pin 3).
  • Check your wires.
  • Ensure code uploaded successfully.
  • Continuous sound (no beeping)?
  • Did you include the delay()? If you don't pause, it might just stay on (or off) so fast you can't tell!

docs.title: 1. The Concept: Digital Input
docs.text:
What are we learning? So far, we have only told the Arduino what to do (Output). Now, we will listen to the Arduino using a Push Button (Input).

We will use a special mode called INPUT_PULLUP.

  • Button Pressed = Signal goes to LOW (0V).
  • Button Released = Signal stays HIGH (5V).

Think of it like a doorbell. When you press it, the circuit connects to the Ground, sending a "LOW" signal that tells the Arduino "I'm pressed!"

docs.text: Push Button LED Arduino Uno Breadboard

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text: We need two circuits here: one for the LED (Output) and one for the Button (Input).

docs.title: A. The LED (Output)
docs.text:
1. Positive (Long Leg) -> Pin 6
  2. Negative (Short Leg) -> GND

docs.title: B. The Button (Input)
docs.text:
Buttons have 4 legs, but we only need to use 2 legs diagonally across from each other (or two on the same side if you are careful).

  1. Connect Leg A to Pin 2.
  2. Connect Leg B to GND.

Note: We don't need a resistor for the button because we are using the Arduino's internal "Pullup" resistor!

(Note: Your wiring might look slightly different depending on which holes you choose, but the connections to Pin 2, Pin 6, and GND must be correct!)

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define our names
const int buttonPin = 2;  // Button is on Pin 2
const int ledPin = 6;     // LED is on Pin 6

void setup() {
  // 2. Set up the LED as visual output
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);

  // 3. Set up the Button as Input with internal Pullup resistor
  // This is IMPORTANT: It keeps the signal HIGH when not pressed.
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
}

void loop() {
  // 4. Read the button state
  // Remember: LOW means pressed!
  int isPressed = digitalRead(buttonPin);

  if (isPressed == LOW) {
    // Button is pushed! Turn ON LED.
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH); 
  } else {
    // Button is not pushed. Turn OFF LED.
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
  }
}

docs.title: Explaining the Logic
docs.text:
• pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP); -> This is the secret sauce. It sets the pin to be HIGH (5V) by default.
  • if (isPressed == LOW) -> When we connect the button to GND (press it), the voltage drops to LOW. So LOW actually means "Action happening"!

docs.text:

  2. Click Upload.

  4. Release the button. Does it turn off?

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• LED is ON when I'm NOT pressing the button?
  • You might have confused the logic. Check if you wrote if (isPressed == HIGH).
  • Or, you might be using INPUT instead of INPUT_PULLUP.
  • Nothing happens?
  • Check the LED wiring (Long leg to Pin 6).
  • Check the Button wiring (One leg to Pin 2, other to GND).
  • Try pressing the button firmly.

docs.title: 1. The Concept: Mixing Colors
docs.text:
What is this? An RGB LED is special. It is not just one light, it is three lights in one package!

  • R = Red
  • G = Green
  • B = Blue

By turning them on at different brightness levels, we can mix them to create ANY color (like Purple, Yellow, or White).

To do this, we need to use special pins on the Arduino called PWM Pins (Pins with the ~ symbol).

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text: RGB LED Arduino Uno Breadboard

docs.title: 3. Standard Wiring (Important!)
docs.text:
Note: The images in this guide might show different pins. Please follow the table below to ensure you can mix colors properly!

We will use Pins 3, 5, and 6 because they support "Color Mixing" (PWM).

RGB Pin Connection Arduino Pin - (Minus) Ground GND R Red Signal Pin 3 G Green Signal Pin 5 B Blue Signal Pin 6

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define our color pins
const int redPin = 3;
const int greenPin = 5;
const int bluePin = 6;

void setup() {
  // 2. Set them all to OUTPUT
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 3. Red Only
  setColor(255, 0, 0); // Red ON, Green OFF, Blue OFF
  delay(1000);

  // 4. Green Only
  setColor(0, 255, 0);
  delay(1000);

  // 5. Blue Only
  setColor(0, 0, 255);
  delay(1000);

  // 6. Mix: Yellow (Red + Green)
  setColor(255, 255, 0);
  delay(1000);

  // 7. Mix: Purple (Red + Blue)
  setColor(255, 0, 255);
  delay(1000);
}

// Helper function to make setting colors easy
void setColor(int red, int green, int blue) {
  analogWrite(redPin, red);
  analogWrite(greenPin, green);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blue);
}

docs.title: Explaining analogWrite
docs.text:
• digitalWrite only does ON (5V) or OFF (0V).
  • analogWrite allows us to choose a value between 0 (Off) and 255 (Full Brightness).
  • By mixing red=255, green=0, blue=255, we get Purple!

docs.title: 5. Upload & Test
docs.text:
1. Verify and Upload.
  2. Watch the LED. It should cycle through Red, Green, Blue, Yellow, Purple.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Colors look wrong? (e.g., Red looks like Blue)
  • You swapped the wires. Check which wire goes to Pin 3, 5, and 6.
  • White light only?
  • You might have connected the - pin to 5V instead of GND. Check the wiring.

docs.title: 1. The Concept: Precision Movement
docs.text:
What are we learning? Normal motors spin around and around (like a fan). Servo Motors are different. They go to a specific angle (like 90°) and STOP. They are used in robot arms, car wipers, and airplane rudders.

To control them, we need a special "Toolbox" of code called a Library. #include <Servo.h>

The Servo has 3 wires attached to it. They are color-coded:

Wire Color Connection Arduino Pin Brown (or Black) Ground GND Red Power 5V Orange (or Yellow) Signal Pin 10

Caution: Do not force the servo arm with your hands. You might break the gears!

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Grab the "Toolbox" for servos
#include <Servo.h> 

// 2. Give our servo a name
Servo myArm; 

void setup() {
  // 3. Tell Arduino where the servo is connected (Pin 10)
  myArm.attach(10);
}

void loop() {
  // 4. Move to 0 degrees
  myArm.write(0);
  delay(1000); // Wait 1 second

  // 5. Move to 90 degrees
  myArm.write(90);
  delay(1000);

  // 6. Move to 180 degrees (Max)
  myArm.write(180);
  delay(1000);
}

docs.title: Explaining the Library
docs.text:
• #include <Servo.h>: This tells the computer "I am using a Servo, please load the special commands".
  • myArm.attach(10): This connects the software "myArm" to the hardware "Pin 10".
  • myArm.write(90): This acts like the steering wheel. It tells the servo exactly where to point.

  • Moves nicely but stops working? Ensure wires are tight. Servos vibrate a lot and can shake wires loose!

1. The Concept: Distance & Color
docs.text:
What are we learning? In this project, we will combine an input (Ultrasonic Sensor) and an output (RGB Module). We will learn how to make decisions using if/else statements.

  • If an object is close, the light turns RED (Danger!).
  • If an object is far away, the light turns GREEN (Safe).

This is the same logic used in car reversing sensors!

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text: Component Quantity Arduino Uno 1 Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04) 1 RGB Module 1 Jumper Wires (Male-to-Female & Male-to-Male) ~8 USB Cable 1

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text: We need to connect two modules. Use the breadboard to make it easier.

docs.title: Ultrasonic Sensor Connections
docs.text:
• VCC -> Arduino 5V
  • GND -> Arduino GND
  • Trig -> Arduino Pin 9
  • Echo -> Arduino Pin 10

docs.title: RGB Module Connections
docs.text:
• R (Red) -> Arduino Pin 3
  • G (Green) -> Arduino Pin 5
  • B (Blue) -> Arduino Pin 6
  • - (GND) -> Arduino GND

Checkpoint: Check your connections carefully! The Ultrasonic sensor needs 5V to work.

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy the code below into your Arduino IDE.

// Define Pins
const int trigPin = 9;
const int echoPin = 10;
const int redPin = 3;
const int greenPin = 5;
const int bluePin = 6;

// Variables for distance
long duration;
int distance;

void setup() {
  // Set up the Ultrasonic Sensor pins
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT); // Sends the sound wave
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);  // Listens for the echo

  // Set up the RGB LED pins
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);

  // Start Serial Monitor (so we can see the distance on screen)
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  // 1. Clear the trigPin
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);

  // 2. Send a 10 microsecond pulse to trigger the sensor
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  // 3. Measure the duration of the echo
  duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);

  // 4. Calculate distance in cm
  distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;

  // Print distance to Serial Monitor
  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.println(distance);

  // 5. Logic: Change color based on distance
  if (distance < 10) {
    // Too close! Turn RED
    setColor(255, 0, 0); 
  } else if (distance < 20) {
    // Getting closer... Turn BLUE/YELLOW
    setColor(0, 0, 255);
  } else {
    // Safe distance. Turn GREEN
    setColor(0, 255, 0);
  }
}

// Helper function to set color easily
void setColor(int red, int green, int blue) {
  analogWrite(redPin, red);
  analogWrite(greenPin, green);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blue);
}

  3. Move your hand in front of the ultrasonic sensor.
    • Close (< 10cm): LED should be Red.
    • Medium (10-20cm): LED should be Blue.
    • Far (> 20cm): LED should be Green.

docs.title: 1. The Concept
docs.text:
We will create an Automatic Street Light that turns on when it gets dark.

  • Bright Light: LED is OFF.
  • Darkness: LED turns ON (White/Yellow).

We use a Photoresistor (LDR) to measure light intensity.

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text:
• Arduino Uno
  • LDR Sensor Module
  • RGB LED Module
  • Jumper Wires

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text:
Standard Wiring: RGB uses Pins 3, 5, 6 for color mixing.

Component Pin Label Arduino Pin RGB LED R (Red) Pin 3 G (Green) Pin 5 B (Blue) Pin 6 - (GND) GND LDR Sensor VCC 5V GND GND AO (Analog) A0

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define Pins
const int redPin = 3;
const int greenPin = 5;
const int bluePin = 6;
const int ldrPin = A0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // 2. Configure Output Pins
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 3. Read Light Level (0 to 1023)
  int lightLevel = analogRead(ldrPin);

  Serial.print("Light Level: ");
  Serial.println(lightLevel);

  // 4. Logic: Dark vs Bright
  // (Adjust '500' based on your room's light)
  if (lightLevel < 500) { 
    // DARK: Turn ON (White Light)
    setColor(255, 255, 255);
  } else {
    // BRIGHT: Turn OFF
    setColor(0, 0, 0);
  }

  delay(100);
}

// Helper Function
void setColor(int red, int green, int blue) {
  analogWrite(redPin, red);
  analogWrite(greenPin, green);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blue);
}

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Light turns on when it's bright? Your LDR might be wired inversely or you need to flip logic < to >.
  • Is it too sensitive? Change the number 500. Higher number = turns on sooner (in brighter light). Lower number = needs to be darker.
  • Colors are wrong? Check RGB wiring (3, 5, 6).

docs.title: 1. The Concept
docs.text:
We will simulate a "Smart Traffic Light" that changes based on traffic density (distance).

  • Car Far Away: Green Light (Flow).
  • Car Approaching: Yellow Light (Caution).
  • Car Stopped (Close): Red Light (Stop).

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text:
• Arduino Uno
  • Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04)
  • Traffic Light Module
  • Jumper Wires

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text:
Standard Wiring: We adhere to the standard pins from Level 1.

Component Pin Label Arduino Pin Traffic Light R (Red) Pin 5 Y (Yellow) Pin 6 G (Green) Pin 7 GND GND Ultrasonic VCC 5V GND GND Trig Pin 12 Echo Pin 11

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define Pins
const int redPin = 5;
const int yellowPin = 6;
const int greenPin = 7;

const int trigPin = 12;
const int echoPin = 11;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // 2. Configure Traffic Light
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(yellowPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);

  // 3. Configure Ultrasonic
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 4. Measure Distance
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  long duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);
  int distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;

  Serial.print("Distance: ");

We will build a "Smart Parking Assistant".

  • Getting close (< 20cm): Light turns RED (Warning!).

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define Pins
const int redPin = 3;
const int greenPin = 5;
const int bluePin = 6;

const int trigPin = 12;
const int echoPin = 11;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600); // Start serial communication

  // 2. Configure RGB Output
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);

  // 3. Configure Ultrasonic Sensor
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // 4. Measure Distance
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  long duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);
  int distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;

  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.print(distance);
  Serial.println(" cm");

  // 5. Logic: Close vs Far
  if (distance < 20) {
    // Too Close! Show RED
    setColor(255, 0, 0); 
  } else {
    // Safe! Show GREEN
    setColor(0, 255, 0); 
  }

  delay(100);
}

// Helper Function
void setColor(int red, int green, int blue) {
  analogWrite(redPin, red);
  analogWrite(greenPin, green);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blue);
}

1. The Concept
docs.text: We will create a Color Cycle light. Every time you press the button, the RGB LED changes color: Red -> Green -> Blue -> OFF -> (Repeat)

docs.title: 2. Components Needed
docs.text:
• Arduino Uno
  • Push Button
  • RGB LED Module
  • Jumper Wires

docs.title: 3. Wiring the Circuit
docs.text:
Standard Wiring: We adhere to the standard pins to ensure reliability.

Component Pin Label Arduino Pin RGB LED R (Red) Pin 3 G (Green) Pin 5 B (Blue) Pin 6 - (GND) GND Button Leg A Pin 2 Leg B GND

docs.title: 4. The Code
docs.text:
Copy this code into your Arduino IDE.

// 1. Define Pins
const int buttonPin = 2;
const int redPin = 3;
const int greenPin = 5;
const int bluePin = 6;

// Variables to store state
int buttonState = 0;       // Current reading
int lastButtonState = 0;   // Previous reading
int colorMode = 0;         // 0=Red, 1=Green, 2=Blue, 3=OFF

void setup() {
  // 2. Configure Output Pins (RGB)
  pinMode(redPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(bluePin, OUTPUT);

  // 3. Configure Input Pin (Button)
  // We use INPUT_PULLUP so we don't need a resistor!
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT_PULLUP);
}

void loop() {
  // 4. Read the button
  buttonState = digitalRead(buttonPin);

  // 5. Detect a "Click" (Transition from HIGH to LOW)
  if (buttonState == LOW && lastButtonState == HIGH) {
    colorMode++; // Go to next color
    if (colorMode > 3) {
      colorMode = 0; // Reset back to start
    }
    delay(200); // Debounce (wait a bit to prevent double clicks)
  }

  lastButtonState = buttonState; // Remember for next loop

  // 6. Set Color based on Mode
  if (colorMode == 0) {
    setColor(255, 0, 0); // RED
  } else if (colorMode == 1) {
    setColor(0, 255, 0); // GREEN
  } else if (colorMode == 2) {
    setColor(0, 0, 255); // BLUE
  } else {
    setColor(0, 0, 0);   // OFF
  }
}

// Helper Function
void setColor(int red, int green, int blue) {
  analogWrite(redPin, red);
  analogWrite(greenPin, green);
  analogWrite(bluePin, blue);
}

docs.text:
• Button doesn't work? Ensure one leg is on Pin 2 and the non-connected leg is on GND. We use INPUT_PULLUP code to make this simple wiring work.
  • Colors don't change? Try pressing the button firmly. The debounce delay helps prevent accidental double-clicks.

// Include comments to explain the code
const int trigPin = 9;    // Trigger pin of ultrasonic sensor
const int echoPin = 10;   // Echo pin of ultrasonic sensor
const int redLed = 6;     // Pin connected to Red LED
const int greenLed = 7;   // Pin connected to Green LED

long duration;  // Variable to store duration of sound wave travel
int distance;   // Variable to store distance calculated

void setup() {
  // Set up the pins as input or output
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);
  pinMode(redLed, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenLed, OUTPUT);

  // Start serial communication
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  // Clear the trigPin by setting it LOW
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);

  // Set the trigPin HIGH for 10 microseconds
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  // Read the echoPin, and calculate the distance
  duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);
  distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;  // Convert to distance in cm

  // Print the distance to the Serial Monitor
  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.print(distance);
  Serial.println(" cm");

  // LED control based on distance
  if (distance < 10) {  // If object is within 10 cm
    digitalWrite(redLed, HIGH);  // Turn on Red LED
    digitalWrite(greenLed, LOW); // Turn off Green LED
  } else {
    digitalWrite(redLed, LOW);   // Turn off Red LED
    digitalWrite(greenLed, HIGH); // Turn on Green LED
  }

  // Delay to allow for stable readings
  delay(500);
}

Step 1: Open your Arduino IDE. See how to set up here: Getting Started.

Step 2: Write the following codes as flows. 

const int trigPin = 9;    // Ultrasonic Sensor Trig Pin
const int echoPin = 10;   // Ultrasonic Sensor Echo Pin
const int redLed = 6;     // Red Light
const int yellowLed = 7;  // Yellow Light
const int greenLed = 8;   // Green Light

// Variables for Distance Measurement
long duration;
int distance;

void setup() {
  // Initialize Sensor Pins
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);

  // Initialize Traffic Light Pins
  pinMode(redLed, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(yellowLed, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(greenLed, OUTPUT);

  // Begin Serial Communication (for debugging)
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  // Measure distance using the ultrasonic sensor
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);
  delayMicroseconds(2);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);

  // Calculate the distance in cm
  duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);
  distance = duration * 0.034 / 2;

  // Print the distance to the Serial Monitor
  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.print(distance);
  Serial.println(" cm");

  // Control the Traffic Light Based on Distance
  if (distance <= 10) { // Vehicle detected close to the intersection
    digitalWrite(redLed, HIGH);   // Red Light ON
    digitalWrite(yellowLed, LOW);
    digitalWrite(greenLed, LOW);
    delay(5000); // Wait for 5 seconds

  } else { // No vehicle detected or vehicle is far
    digitalWrite(redLed, LOW);
    digitalWrite(yellowLed, LOW);
    digitalWrite(greenLed, HIGH); // Green Light ON
    delay(5000); // Wait for 5 seconds

    digitalWrite(greenLed, LOW);
    digitalWrite(yellowLed, HIGH); // Yellow Light ON
    delay(2000); // Wait for 2 seconds
    digitalWrite(yellowLed, LOW);
  }
}

Your journey into STEM starts here!

The STEMAIDE Kit is your toolkit for building the future. With over 200 possible projects, you will learn how to control lights, make sounds, sense the environment, and build smart systems.

This guide will help you set up your computer so you can start programming your STEMAIDE board immediately.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
Before we begin, make sure you have:

  1. A Laptop or Desktop Computer (Windows, Mac, or Linux).
  2. The STEMAIDE Kit (specifically the Arduino Uno board and the blue USB cable).
  3. Curiosity!

docs.title: 1. Setting Up the Software (Arduino IDE)
docs.text:
The Arduino IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is the software we use to write code and send it to the board. Think of it as a text editor that talks to hardware.

Step 1: Open the Software Double-click the Arduino IDE icon on your computer.

Step 2: The Interface When it opens, you will see a window like this. This is where you will write your code.

docs.title: Key Areas to Know
docs.text:
• void setup(): This runs once when you turn on the board. We use it to tell the board what devices are connected (like "I have an LED on pin 6").
  • void loop(): This runs forever in a circle. This is where the magic happens (like "Turn LED on... wait... turn off").

docs.title: 2. Preparing the Code Space
docs.text:
To make coding easier, let's make some space. Click before void setup() and press Enter a few times to create a blank space at the top.

Why? We use this top space to give names to our pins (e.g., int led = 6;). It makes code easier to read!

docs.title: 3. Comments (Notes for Humans)
docs.text:
You will often see lines starting with //. These are Comments.

  • The computer ignores them.
  • They are there to help YOU understand what the code does.
// This is a comment. It does nothing to the board.
pinMode(6, OUTPUT); // This sets pin 6 as an output

docs.title: 4. Connecting Your Board
docs.text:
Now, let's connect your STEMAIDE board to the computer.

Step 1: Plug it in Connect the blue USB cable to the Arduino and your USB port.

Step 2: Select Board Go to Tools > Board > Arduino Uno.

Step 3: Select Port Go to Tools > Port and select the one that says Arduino Uno (e.g., COM3, COM5, /dev/tty...).

Note: If you don't see "Arduino Uno" next to a port, try unplugging and replugging the cable.

docs.title: 5. Saving & Uploading
docs.text:
Once you have written code (we'll do that in the next chapter!), you need to send it to the board.

  1. Verify (Check): Click the Checkmark icon. This checks for spelling mistakes in your code.
  2. Upload (Send): Click the Arrow icon. This sends the code to the board.

Success! When you see "Done uploading" at the bottom, your code is running on the board!

docs.text:
This guide is for Educators, Engineers, and Advanced Students who want to add new projects to the STEMAIDE Kit documentation. We call these "Missions".

Goal: Transform complex electronic concepts into engaging, story-driven challenges.

docs.title: 1. The Narrative Structure
docs.text:
Every new project must follow the Innovator's Journey format:

  1. The Call to Adventure (Problem): What real-world problem are we solving? (e.g., Dark streets, Crashes).
  2. The Toolkit (Components): What parts do we need?
  3. The Blueprint (Wiring): Clear diagrams.
  4. The Logic (Code): Explain the concept, not just the syntax.
  5. The Debrief (Challenge): A follow-up task to test understanding.

docs.title: 2. Style Guide
docs.text:
• Tone: Encouraging, Professional, African-Centric.
  • Role: Treat the reader as a "Lead Engineer" or "Innovator", not a student.
  • Code: Use clear variable names (int redPin = 5 NOT int r = 5).

docs.title: 3. How to Submit
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository.
  2. Create a new Markdown file in the appropriate Level folder (e.g., 3.0/3.7.Smart_Irrigation).
  3. Images: Put diagrams in assets/.
  4. Submit a Pull Request.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This handbook is your field guide to the STEMAIDE Kit. While the "Missions" (Level 1, 2, 3) teach you how to build specific projects, this guide provides the technical reference data you might need along the way.

docs.title: 1. Safety First
docs.text:
Before you build, remember the Innovator's Code:

  1. Never connect wires while the board is plugged into the computer.
  2. Double-check your wiring (especially VCC and GND) before powering up.
  3. Keep it tidy. A messy circuit is hard to debug.

docs.title: Digital Outputs (Actuators)
docs.text:
• LEDs: Light Emitting Diodes. Beware of polarity (Long leg is +).
  • Buzzer: Makes sound. Active buzzers need only 5V; Passive buzzers need a signal.
  • Traffic Light Module: Pins are R, Y, G, GND.

docs.title: Analog Inputs (Sensors)
docs.text:
• LDR (Light Dependent Resistor): Resistance changes with light. Good for "Smart Street Lights".
  • Potentiometer: A knob that changes resistance. Good for dials and volume.

docs.title: Digital Inputs
docs.text: • Push Button: Connects two points when pressed. Use INPUT_PULLUP to make wiring easier.

docs.title: Smart Modules
docs.text:
• Ultrasonic Sensor (HC-SR04): Measures distance using sound. Echolocation!
  • Servo Motor: Moves to a specific angle (0-180 degrees).

docs.title: 3. Common Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"My Code Won't Upload!"

  • Check the USB Cable. Is it plugged in firmly?
  • Check Tools > Board. Is "Arduino Uno" selected?
  • Check Tools > Port. Is the correct COM port selected?

"The circuit isn't working!"

  • Check GND. Is everything connected to Ground?
  • Check Pin Numbers. Did you plug the LED into Pin 6 but program Pin 5?
  • Check Polarity. Are your LEDs plugged in backwards?
